Copywriting Guidelines

Keep It Clear and Concise
	•	Avoid unnecessary words. Give users clear, direct instructions.
	•	Example: Instead of “Your workout will begin shortly,” say “Start workout.”

No Fluff or Hype
	•	Skip generic motivational phrases or vague claims.
	•	Example: Instead of “Unleash your fitness potential,” say “Track your progress.”

Action-Oriented Language
	•	Focus on what users need to do next.
	•	Example: Instead of “You will need to select a training cycle,” say “Choose your training cycle.”

Consistent Formatting and Terminology
	•	Use the same terms throughout the app (e.g., “Training Period” not sometimes “Phase”).
	•	Use numerals for numbers (“3 sets”, not “three sets”).

Be Precise About Features
	•	If something needs to be set up, say so.
	•	If a feature isn’t available, specify when it’s coming or suggest an alternative.

No Redundant Information
	•	Don’t repeat what’s already clear.
	•	Example: Instead of “You are viewing your workout plan,” just show the plan and next steps.

Make Buttons and Actions Clear
	•	“Start” → “Begin Workout” (if a session is about to start).
	•	“Edit” → “Edit Plan” (for clarity).
	•	Buttons should use title case.

Use a Neutral, Professional Tone
	•	Avoid overly casual or intense language unless intentional.
	•	Example: Instead of “Crush your workout!” say “Complete your session.”

Anticipate User Questions
	•	If something could be unclear, address it up front.
	•	Example: If progress tracking is coming soon, say “Progress tracking (Coming soon). Contact support for alternatives.”

Keep Help Text Integrated
	•	Place help text close to the relevant feature or embed it as a bullet point.

Avoid Ambiguous Timeframes
	•	Be specific about when things will happen.
	•	Example: Instead of “Your plan will update soon,” say “Plan updates in 10 seconds.”

Use User-Centered Language
	•	Focus on what the user can do, not what the system does.
	•	Example: Instead of “Workouts are being generated,” say “Your workout is ready.”

Don’t Assume Prior Knowledge
	•	If using training terms, briefly explain or link to more info.
	•	Example: Instead of “Start your mesocycle,” say “Start your training period (multi-week block).”

Default to Positive, Supportive Language
	•	Frame messages in an encouraging, solution-focused way, even for errors.
	•	Example: Instead of “Workout failed to save,” say “Couldn’t save workout. Try again or contact support.”

Minimize Distractions During Key Actions
	•	Keep the user focused during important steps like starting or confirming a plan.

Write Helpful Error Messages
	•	Explain what happened and how to fix it.
	•	Example: Instead of “Invalid input,” say “Enter a valid number of sets.”

Keep Confirmation Messages Clear
	•	Let users know what happens next after an action.
	•	Example: Instead of “Workout logged,” say “Workout saved. View progress in your dashboard.”

Keep Form Labels Simple
	•	Labels should be short and clear.
	•	Placeholder text should not repeat the label.
	•	Example: Label: “Goal” → Input Placeholder: “e.g. Increase endurance”

Ensure All Call-to-Action (CTA) Buttons Are Specific
	•	Every button should describe the action.
	•	Example: Instead of “Submit”, use “Save Workout”.

Keep It Short, Not Cryptic
	•	Use the fewest words possible without losing clarity.
	•	Example: Instead of “Your workout plan is being generated and will be available soon,” say “Generating your plan…”

Prioritize Clarity Over Cleverness
	•	Avoid jargon unless your audience already knows it.
	•	Example: Instead of “Microcycles are updating,” say “Weekly plans are updating.”

Show, Don’t Tell
	•	If an action is obvious from the UI, don’t repeat it.
	•	Let labels, buttons, and structure guide the user.

Use Sentence Case Everywhere
	•	Except for buttons and links.
	•	Example: “View workout history” not “View Workout History”

Error Messages Should Be Helpful, Not Alarming
	•	Explain what happened and how to fix it.
	•	Example: Instead of “Error 503: Something went wrong,” say “Server is temporarily unavailable. Try again in a few minutes.”

CTA Buttons Should Be Actionable
	•	Buttons should clearly describe the action.
	•	Example: “Start Workout”, “Log Progress”

Use Progressive Disclosure for Advanced Features
	•	Don’t overload users with details up front.
	•	Show advanced options only when needed.

Default to a Professional, Neutral Tone
	•	Avoid sounding too robotic or too casual.
	•	Keep personality subtle and let design add warmth.

Confirm Actions with Context
	•	When users take an important action, confirm it.
	•	Example: After saving a plan, show “Plan saved. Begin your first workout.”

Avoid Passive Voice
	•	Make copy direct and active.
	•	Example: Instead of “Workout has been logged,” say “You logged your workout.”

Keep the UI Copy Consistent
	•	Use the same terms throughout for features and actions.

Assume the User Knows What They’re Doing
	•	Don’t over-explain basic fitness concepts—link to more info if needed.

If It’s Not Necessary, Remove It
	•	Every extra word adds friction.
	•	Example: Instead of “Your workout is now complete and you can view your results,” say “Workout complete.”
